Learning Objectives
Review the unique characteristics of the geriatric population and explain how these
characteristics predispose geriatric patients to injuries and affects their recovery and
outcomes.
Explain the unique vascular supply to the femoral head and how it affects treatment decisions.
Discuss how patient age influences treatment goals and special considerations in the geriatric
population.
Describe the manner in which fracture characteristics guide implant selection and predispose
patients to complications.


Overview
Older adults represent a growing, unique patient population, with special considerations
with regard to surgical indications, surgical goals, perioperative treatment and workup,
and complications that result from surgical treatment or the initial trauma.
Epidemiology
Given the increasing older adult population, the incidence of hip fractures likely will increase in
the coming decades.

Epidemiology
The growing middle-aged (55 to 64 years) and geriatric (older than 65 years) populations
have led to a drastic increase in the incidence of geriatric trauma, including hip fractures.
Hip fractures are more common in women, and the risk and incidence increase with
decreasing bone mass, highlighting the importance of preventative medicine in patients
with known osteoporosis. The current geriatric population consists of approximately
43.1 million individuals and is expected to double to 83.7 million individuals by 2050. The
current burden of geriatric trauma in the overall trauma population is 12%; that
percentage is expected to continue increase to an estimated 40% by 2040 as this patient
population grows. This growth will place a stress on hospital system resources;
therefore, knowledge of the factors contributing to the treatment of elderly patients who
sustain trauma is paramount to maintaining quality care.1
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The osseous anatomy of the femoral neck and head is complex, and the orientation of cortical
and cancellous bone has certain implications with regard to fracture patterns and

classification.
The head-neck angle, canal diameter, and femoral bow all contribute to reduction
intraoperatively and the type of implant for fixation.
The typical femoral neck orientation is 15° of anteversion, with a neck-shaft angle of 125° to
127°.
The Dorr index describes the canal diameter2 (Figure 1).
Figure 1 AP hip radiographs demonstrate the Dorr classification system, which serves as a
descriptor of femoral morphology and bone quality. Type A femurs have a narrow canal with
thick cortical walls (champagne flute canal). Type B femurs have moderate cortical walls. Type
C femurs have a wide canal with thin cortical walls (stove-pipe canal). (Reproduced from Siddiqi
A, Springer BD, Chen AF, Piuzzi NS: Diagnosis and management of intraoperative fractures in
primary total hip arthroplasty. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2021;29[10]:e497-e512.)

Osteology
The femoral head and neck consist of cortical and cancellous bone. Two primary
trabecular groups exist, the principal tensile and compressive groups and secondary
groups. These patterns form because of the reaction of bone to stress, known as the
Wolff law. The Ward triangle, which is a radiolucent area contained within the principal
compressive group, principal tensile group, and secondary compressive group, is

9/3/26, 4:18 PM
AAOS | Geriatric Hip Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000535
3/59

thought to be the weakest area of the proximal femur and is a common area of fracture
(Figure 2). The medial area of dense trabecular bone that transfers stress from the
inferior aspect of the femoral neck to the shaft is known as the calcar femorale.
Figure 2 Drawing shows the trabecular groups of the proximal femur. W = Ward triangle
(Adapted with permission from Singh M, Nagrath AR, Maini PS: Changes in trabecular
pattern of the upper end of the femur as an index of osteoporosis. J Bone Joint Surg Am
1970;52[3]:457-467.)
The degree of femoral bowing is important to determine in managing intertrochanteric
femur fractures with the use of a cephalomedullary nail. If a long, straight stem is
selected for a patient with increased femoral bowing, it may increase the risk of anterior
cortex perforation distally. In addition, the Dorr index is used to evaluate the femoral
canal diameter. The Dorr index is the ratio of the femoral canal diameter at the level of
the lesser trochanter to the diameter at a point 10 cm distal to the lesser trochanter.
This classification system can help guide nail sizing and arthroplasty implant selection
and the optimal location of fixation in the femur.
In most patients, the femoral neck is in approximately 15° of anteversion in relation to
the posterior aspect of the femoral condyles distally. The femoral head-neck junction
angle or neck-shaft angle is 125° to 127°. These parameters must be considered in
assessing the alignment of intertrochanteric femur fractures during reduction and
fixation. Avoiding varus alignment is key because it leads to an increased risk of
complications, including screw cutout. During arthroplasty, the surgeon should consider
that the center of the femoral head usually is located at the level of the tip of the greater
trochanter. This may aid in assessing length and offset obtained intraoperatively during

fractures.3
Vascular Anatomy
The main blood supply to the femoral head arises from the lateral ascending branches of the
medial femoral circumflex artery.
Disruption of these vessels in patients with a femoral neck fracture increases the risk of
femoral head osteonecrosis.
The blood supply also must be considered during the fixation of femoral neck fractures to
prevent osteonecrosis, particularly in younger patients.
The femoral head also receives vascularity from the lateral femoral circumflex artery.
In addition, the common femoral artery, profunda femoral artery, and superior and inferior
gluteal arteries must be considered during approaches to the hip.
Figure 3 shows a diagram of the acetabulum and other vascular structures at risk during screw
placement to secure the acetabular component in arthroplasty.

Nerve injuries in total hip arthroplasty. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1999;7[2]:101-111.)

Vascular Anatomy
The main blood supply to the femoral head arises from the medial femoral circumflex
artery. It terminates in the posterior aspect of the extracapsular arterial ring, which gives
off the ascending cervical arteries. The lateral group of these ascending branches is
thought to be the main blood supply to the femoral head, giving off the lateral
epiphyseal artery, which penetrates the femoral head as its dominant blood supply.
Disruption of these ascending cervical branches in patients with a femoral neck fracture
increases the risk of femoral head osteonecrosis.

The lateral femoral circumflex artery terminates in the anterior aspect of the arterial
ring, which also receives contributions from the superior and inferior gluteal arteries
(Figure 4). The artery of the ligamentum teres has variable contributions from the medial
femoral circumflex artery and the obturator artery. Although important in childhood, the
artery of the ligamentum teres does not provide adequate blood supply to the adult
femoral head to maintain viability.
The common femoral artery arises from the external iliac artery as it passes deep to the
inguinal ligament. It courses anterior and medial to the hip capsule. Similarly, the
common femoral vein is a continuation of the external iliac vein and courses alongside
the artery. These vascular structures are the most reported extra-pelvic structures
injured during total hip replacement, most often by retractor placement anterior to the
acetabulum. If the surgeon remains lateral to the sartorius muscle during the direct
anterior approach to the hip, these structures should be protected.
The profunda femoral artery arises from the common femoral artery approximately 3.5
cm distal to the inguinal ligament. It travels between the pectineus and adductor longus
muscles and, in most individuals, it gives rise to the lateral and medial femoral
circumflex arteries.3
Additional vascular structures must be considered during screw fixation of the
acetabular component if arthroplasty is selected for the management of hip fracture. If a
screw is placed in the anterior-superior quadrant, the external iliac vessels are at
increased risk of injury; this area typically is deemed inappropriate for screw placement.
The anterior-inferior quadrant also is a danger zone, putting the obturator vessels at risk
for injury. The posterior-inferior quadrant can be used safely, but the inferior gluteal and
pudendal vessels may be at risk if the screws are too long. The safe zone, or the
posterior-superior quadrant, is the optimal location for screws; however, risk of injury to
the superior gluteal vessels exists.

Neural Anatomy
The incidence of nerve injury in geriatric patients with a hip fracture is low; however, nerve
injuries can occur, and a thorough neurovascular examination should be performed.
This neurovascular examination also is an important aspect of the preoperative evaluation
because approaches to the hip may increase the risk of injury to neural structures.
Nerves to consider include the sciatic nerve, the femoral nerve, the lateral femoral cutaneous
nerve (LFCN), and the superior and inferior gluteal nerves.

The sciatic nerve is most at risk during posterior approaches to the hip, whereas the femoral
nerve and the LFCN are more commonly injured during the anterior approach.
A diagram of the acetabulum is shown in Figure 3. In placing screws during cup placement
for total hip arthroplasty (THA), the sciatic, superior and inferior gluteal, obturator, and
pudendal nerves must be considered.

Neural Anatomy
The sciatic nerve originates from the lumbosacral plexus (L4 through S3). It exits the
pelvis through the greater sciatic notch and lies anterior to the piriformis in most
individuals. This anatomy is important to understand during the posterior approach to
the hip. The femoral nerve is formed by branches arising from L2 through L4 (Figure 5).
It courses on top of the iliopsoas muscle, passing anterior and medial to the hip joint
within the femoral triangle. The borders of the femoral triangle consist of the inguinal
ligament proximally, the sartorius muscle laterally, and the adductor longus muscle
medially. From lateral to medial, surgeons will encounter the nerve, the artery, and then
the femoral vein. The LFCN passes deep to the inguinal ligament as it courses into the
anterior thigh. This structure is important in the anterior approach to the hip.3

Tendons and Musculature
The musculature about the hip contributes to fracture displacement patterns and must be
considered in the reduction of proximal femur fractures.
Subtrochanteric femur fractures characteristically present with the proximal fragment flexed,
abducted, and externally rotated because of the pull of the external rotators, abductors, and
iliopsoas.
Intertrochanteric femur fractures present with more variable displacement patterns,
depending on the stability of the fracture pattern; comminution; and isolated fragments,
such as a separate lesser trochanter fragment.

Hip musculature also contributes to treatment considerations, particularly for arthroplasty.
The hip abductors may play the most important role, with key implications for the risk of
dislocation events after arthroplasty.
These tendons and muscles also serve as important landmarks during approaches to the hip.

Tendons and Musculature
The primary hip flexors are the iliopsoas, rectus femoris, and sartorius muscles.
Secondary flexors include the tensor fascia lata (TFL), pectineus, adductor
longus/brevis/magnus, and gracilis muscles (Figure 6). The iliopsoas has an extensive
origin along the iliac crest and fossa, sacral ala, iliolumbar ligaments, and sacroiliac
ligaments, as well as the bodies and transverse processes of the T12 through L4
vertebrae. It inserts on the lesser trochanter. The rectus femoris crosses both the hip
and knee joints. The straight head originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine,
whereas the reflected head originates from the supraacetabular tubercle of the
acetabulum. It inserts onto the extensor mechanism of the knee through the quadriceps
tendon, patella, and patellar tendon onto the tibial tubercle. The sartorius originates on
the anterior superior iliac spine, again crosses the hip and knee joints, and inserts on the
medial tibia at the pes anserine complex. The TFL muscle originates laterally on the
anterolateral ridge of the iliac crest. These muscle fibers then combine to form the
iliotibial band, which attaches via the Gerdy tubercle to the lateral proximal tibia.

muscles that move the lower leg typically originate on the femur and insert into the

aid in flexing the thigh. The posterior muscles of the femur flex the lower leg but also aid

The gluteus maximus and hamstring muscles are the primary hip extensors. The major
hamstring muscles cross the hip and knee joints, originating on the ischial tuberosity and

inserting in the pes anserine complex. The gluteus maximus originates from the sacrum,
coccyx, and sacrotuberous ligaments. It inserts onto the lateral intramuscular septum.
The primary hip abductors are the gluteus medius and the gluteus minimus. The gluteus
medius has anterior, middle, and posterior components. The gluteus medius and
minimus function together to maintain abduction of the femur during the stance phase
of gait. A Trendelenburg gait refers to a leaning or lurching on the affected side while
walking to compensate for weakness of the hip abductors. Some surgeons have argued
that posterior approaches to the hip that violate the hip abductors may contribute to
postoperative hip instability. Using a direct anterior versus posterior approach to the hip
in the management of femoral neck fractures continues to be a subject of great debate.
The external rotators include the obturator internus and externus, superior and inferior
gemelli, quadratus femoris, and piriformis (Figure 7). The obturator internus originates
on the inner component of the obturator foramen and exits the pelvis through the lesser
sciatic foramen. The gemelli also follow this path. The piriformis exits the pelvis through
the greater sciatic foramen and inserts at the piriformis fossa of the greater trochanter.
This landmark is especially important during the posterior approach to the hip because
the sciatic nerve most often passes below the piriformis and then proceeds to lie on top
of the other short external rotators. Tagging these muscles and tendons and reflecting
them posteriorly protects the nerve during this approach.3

Joints and Ligaments
The hip is a ball and socket joint.
Primary stability results from the osseous anatomy and the fit of the femoral head within the
acetabulum, augmented by the labrum and the hip capsule.


Joints and Ligaments
The hip joint has strong capsular ligaments, the anterior iliofemoral and pubofemoral
ligaments and the posterior ischiofemoral ligaments, which run from the acetabulum to
the femoral neck. The hip capsule attaches to the femur anteriorly along the
intertrochanteric crest. Posteriorly, it attaches only partially, making the basicervical
region of the femoral neck and intertrochanteric region extracapsular. The ligamentum
teres runs from the cotyloid fossa of the acetabulum to the fovea on the femoral head.
In most individuals, the acetabulum is positioned in approximately 45° of abduction
(caudal tilt) and approximately 15° of anteversion (anterior tilt). The anterior and
posterior brims of the acetabulum help determine implant version intraoperatively, and
the base of the fovea helps determine medialization.3 The acetabulum also can be
divided into four quadrants, which aids in acetabular screw placement (Figure 3). The
safest area for screw placement is in the posterior-superior quadrant. Restoration of
joint alignment in geriatric patients with a hip fracture is most important for femoral
neck fractures managed via arthroplasty.
Etiology and Mechanism of Injury
Bimodal mechanism of injury
Young patients: high-energy mechanism of injury
Geriatric patients: low-energy mechanism of injury, usually a ground-level fall

Etiology and Mechanism of Injury
Similar to many fracture types, a bimodal mechanism of injury occurs, leading to
proximal femur fractures. Younger patients tend to present with high-energy
mechanisms of injury, whereas elderly patients tend to present with low-energy trauma.
Most older patients present after a ground-level fall, sustaining a direct blow to the

the capsule results in a proximal femur fracture.
Risk Factors
Risk profiling of the elderly population requires accounting for the energy mechanism, patient
age, physiologic status, injury profile, and comorbidity status.
Traditional risk assessment tools in trauma include the Injury Severity Score (ISS) and the
Trauma Injury Severity Score. The ISS does not account for patient age; the Trauma Injury
Severity Score accounts for patient age.
The Score for Trauma Triage in the Geriatric and Middle-Aged score was created to account for
not only patient age but also physiologic status, injury profile, and comorbidity status.
Osteoporosis also is a major risk factor that plays a role in geriatric trauma.

Risk Factors
Geriatric patients who sustain trauma have a different physiologic profile compared with
younger patients. As patients age, they tend to have an increased number of medical
comorbidities affecting all organ systems, which has a profound effect on the body’s
ability to respond to and compensate for traumatic injuries.
The ISS is a quantitative tool used to characterize the injury profile in a trauma patient. It
comprises six subcomponents recorded as an Abbreviated Injury Scale, including
head/neck, face, chest, abdomen, extremity (including the pelvis), and external (skin)
components. These scores are recorded from 0 to 6; 0 indicates no injury, and 6
indicates an injury not compatible with life. The highest Abbreviated Injury Scale value in
the three most injured subcomponents is taken and squared, followed by the summing
of these values. Typically, an ISS higher than 15 is considered major trauma and is
associated with an inpatient mortality rate of 10%; however, this scoring system does
not consider patient age, physiologic status, or comorbidities.

The Trauma Injury Severity Score differs from the ISS in that it accounts for patient age
as a dichotomous variable, separating patients into two groups: those younger than 55
years and those older than 55 years. It also accounts for a physiologic profile via the
Glasgow Coma Scale, systolic blood pressure, and respiratory rate. This scoring is
associated with moderate predictive utility in geriatric patients who sustain trauma
because it does not account for comorbidities or the energy mechanism.
The Trauma Triage in the Geriatric and Middle-Aged was developed as a tool that
accounts for physiologic status, injury profile, and comorbidities, making it a more
robust tool in the geriatric trauma patient population. It can be used to predict inpatient
mortality risk in patients older than 55 years. It has been validated against the National
Trauma Data Bank and has been used prospectively with great accuracy.1
Osteoporosis also plays an important role in geriatric patients who sustain trauma and
low-energy fractures. Hip fractures are the second most common fragility fracture after
vertebral fractures. An estimated 10 million Americans and more than 200 million
individuals worldwide have osteoporosis, and 1.5 million osteoporotic fractures occur
each year. Given the growing older population, these numbers are expected to increase.
Certain lifestyles, medications, and medical comorbidities also increase the risk of
osteopenia and osteoporosis.
A hip fracture is considered a fragility fracture, and patients should undergo a bone
health work up. These patients have a tenfold increased risk of a second hip fracture and
an associated 20% increased risk of mortality. The key is to identify patients with
osteoporosis and initiate appropriate preventative measures before fracture;
management of osteoporosis should be initiated in all patients with a fragility fracture.4
Associated Injuries
Given that a ground-level fall is a common mechanism of injury in patients with a hip fracture
and patients with a head bleed, intracranial pathology must be considered in any patient who
presents with a hip fracture after a fall.5

Other fragility fractures, including distal radius, proximal humerus, and vertebral compression
fractures, often are associated with the mechanism of injury.

Associated Injuries
A ground-level fall is the most common mechanism of injury leading to geriatric hip
fractures; therefore, the clinician also must evaluate for associated injuries that may be
sustained after a fall. If a patient reports a history of head injury or loss of
consciousness; demonstrates physical signs of head trauma, such as ecchymoses or
lacerations; or presents with an altered mental status, the clinician should order
advanced imaging studies to rule out intracranial hemorrhage. Additional associated
fractures also should be ruled out and evaluated for via appropriate imaging studies
based on the clinical examination.
Injury Classification
Proximal femur fractures are classified based on their anatomic location in relation to the hip
joint capsule.
Femoral neck fractures are considered intracapsular hip fractures, which places them at higher
risk of nonunion given the absence of a periosteal or extraosseous blood supply.
Typically, the authors of this lesson use the Garden classification of femoral neck fractures.
The simplified Garden classification system distinguishes displaced fracture patterns from
nondisplaced fracture patterns, which predicts the risk of osteonecrosis and influences
management.
Intertrochanteric fractures are considered extracapsular hip fractures with a more abundant
blood supply.
They are classified as stable or unstable according to the Evans classification system (Figure
8).
Typically, unstable intertrochanteric femur fractures are those with posteromedial
comminution, reverse obliquity, a thin lateral cortex, or subtrochanteric extension.
Some debate exists regarding basicervical (low) femoral neck fractures. They often are
thought to be extracapsular and behave in a manner similar to intertrochanteric fractures.

Peritrochanteric fracture refers to a fracture about the hip that does not meet or behaves in a
manner similar to a simple intertrochanteric fracture.
Peritrochanteric fractures may extend into the subtrochanteric region or involve the neck
and intertrochanteric region of the proximal femur.
Such fractures require special considerations in surgical planning.

Injury Classification
The classification scheme used most often for femoral neck fractures is the Garden
classification system (Figure 9).6 This system divides fractures into four types. Types I
and II represent nondisplaced fracture patterns, and types III and IV represent displaced

fracture patterns. Type I fractures are nondisplaced, incomplete, valgus impacted
femoral neck fractures. Type II fractures are nondisplaced but complete, with no
disruption in the femoral neck trabecular lines. In Type III fractures, which are complete
with some displacement, the femoral head falls into varus and anterior angulation,
causing the trabecular lines of the femoral head/neck and pelvis to be malaligned. Type
IV fractures are completely displaced, with the femoral head/neck and pelvis trabecular
lines remaining parallel. This classification system provides prognostic information with
regard to the risk of nonunion and osteonecrosis and helps dictate treatment options
(fixation versus arthroplasty). The Pauwels classification system is less widely used6
(Figure 10). This classification system divides fractures into three groups based on the
angle of the fracture. Type I is less than 30° of angulation. Type II is 30° to 50° of
angulation. Type III is greater than 50° of angulation. More vertical fracture patterns may
be at increased risk of nonunion and osteonecrosis. A system often used for research
purposes is the AO Foundation/Orthopaedic Trauma Association classification system.
This classification system differentiates femoral neck fractures based on regions,
including the subcapital, transcervical, and basicervical, and displacement.7
Unstable intertrochanteric fractures are those with posteromedial comminution, reverse
obliquity, a thin lateral cortex, or subtrochanteric extension.

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Surgeons must obtain a thorough patient history because most geriatric patients have
multiple comorbid conditions and surgical risk factors.
The history of the present illness should include the mechanism of injury (syncopal versus
mechanical ground-level fall); the timing of the injury; and evaluation for concomitant injuries,
such as intracranial hemorrhage or other fractures.
The medical history should include a thorough medication reconciliation, specifically with
regard to blood thinners and the last dosage taken.
The medical history and the social history also should include baseline functional status.
Given the high incidence of pre-existing dementia or pain-related delirium, the supplemental

Intertrochanteric Fractures
Goals of fixation include re-establishing a normal femoral neck-shaft angle and allowing for
some controlled collapse/compression at the fracture site.
Reduction is performed on a fracture table with hip flexion, adduction, internal rotation, and
traction.
Typically, stable intertrochanteric fractures are managed with the use of an SHS.
The use of an SHS is an extra-medullary technique.
Advantages include easy application, wide availability, high success rates, and low cost.
Disadvantages include requiring an open technique with increased blood loss, increased
failure rates in unstable fracture patterns (particularly lateral wall fractures), and increased
fracture deformity in unstable fracture patterns.
Unstable fracture patterns are better managed via cephalomedullary nailing.
Advantages of nailing include percutaneous application with decreased blood loss; lateral
buttressing, limiting collapse and subsequent fracture deformity, even in unstable patterns;
and increased resistance to varus forces.
Disadvantages include increased incidence of screw cutout and increased implant cost (
Video 6).
Femoral head lag screw placement should be in the center of the head with fixation in
subchondral bone.
A tip-apex distance greater than 25 mm is associated with increased rates of screw cutout.
Slight inferior placement on AP radiographs may lead to greater axial and torsional
stiffness.
No substantial difference between screw fixation and helical blade fixation has been
observed; however, cadaver model studies have shown increased rotational and
translational stiffness with the use of helical blades.30

Intertrochanteric femur fractures usually are managed with the use of an SHS or a

via nailing are believed to result in better outcomes. Unstable fracture patterns include
those with a thin lateral wall or lateral cortical buttress, posteromedial comminution,

the fracture site against the lateral plate.31 Studies have shown that a lateral wall
thickness of less than 21 mm may predispose patients to this complication.32

Reduction is another important aspect of management. Typically, a varus reduction puts
more load and stress on the implant, which is less of a problem with intramedullary
devices, which can bear greater loads. If using an SHS, valgus reduction is key. In
addition to a thin lateral cortical buttress, posteromedial comminution also should be
considered. In simple fracture patterns with one fracture line exiting medially, the
cortices can be realigned to allow for compression through medial cortical bone. This is
amenable to SHS fixation; however, if several fracture lines exit medially or if the lesser
trochanter exists as a separate fragment, intramedullary fixation should be
considered.31
In addition, cost must be considered. Intramedullary implants cost 20% to 40% more
than SHSs. Simple fracture patterns should be managed with the less expensive device,
if appropriate. Another consideration is whether to use a short or long nail if using an
intramedullary device. Longer nails tend to cost up to 45% more than short nails;
however, some studies have shown considerably higher complication rates with short
nail fixation, particularly because of periprosthetic fracture.33 Some surgeons support
using a long nail to protect the entire femur. No good evidence currently exists to
strongly support one method or the other.31
Femoral head fixation can be attained via screw fixation or blade fixation. Biomechanical
studies have shown better resistance to rotational and translational stresses with a
blade; however, no additional evidence has shown an actual difference in cutout rates,
complications, or postoperative functional outcomes. The tip-apex distance may be
more important (Figure 16). Baumgaertner et al34 reported that a tip-apex distance of
25 mm or less was associated with a decreased risk of implant cutout. This distance is
measured by summing the distance from the tip of the lag screw to the apex of the
femoral head on an AP radiograph and a lateral radiograph. Additional studies also have
shown a biomechanical advantage of slightly inferior lag screw placement.35 Inferior
placement on AP radiographs with central placement on lateral radiographs produces
the highest axial and torsional load resistance.35

subtrochanteric femur fractures. Research typically supports this construct only in

Postoperative complications in the geriatric patient who sustain adversely affect the outcomes
surgical management.1
Interdisciplinary management is imperative until safe hospital discharge.
Delirium
Altered postoperative mental status has been associated with increased mortality.1
It may be classified as postoperative delirium or postoperative cognitive dysfunction.
Multiple risk factors for delirium: infection, dehydration, hypoperfusion, medications
(narcotics, antihistamines, benzodiazepines), baseline dementia, physical restraints
Management includes identifying and correcting the underlying etiology.
Medical management may include haloperidol and/or low-dose lorazepam as a last option.
Pulmonary complications
The most common complications are atelectasis and pneumonia.1
Atelectasis usually presents on postoperative day two to five, with increased work of
breathing, low-grade fever, and hypoxemia. Management may include incentive spirometer
usage, suctioning, and chest physiotherapy; however, mobilization is key.
Pneumonia may present from postoperative day zero to five and is associated with fever and
new infiltrates observed on chest radiographs. Management consists of sputum and blood
cultures and initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotic agents, with tailoring of organism-specific
antibiotic agents after culture results are finalized.
Postoperative cardiac complications
Postoperative cardiac complications can be risk stratified via the Revised Cardiac Risk Index,
mostly evaluated by the geriatric/medicine team.1
Major cardiac events include myocardial infarction, arrhythmias (eg, atrial fibrillation), and
heart failure.
Postoperative myocardial infarction may present as a silent myocardial infarction in elderly
patients with cardiac risk factors because only one-third of these patients present with
classic chest pain.
Workup should include serial troponins every 8 hours for as long as 24 hours along with
electrocardiography.
Postoperative atrial fibrillation, the most common arrhythmia, is problematic because it may
cause mental status changes and syncope. Patients may be symptomatic (heart palpitations)
or asymptomatic. The diagnosis is performed via electrocardiography, and management
focuses on a rate-control strategy, which has shown a trend toward reduction in all-cause
mortality.

Acute postoperative heart failure should warrant suspicion for myocardial ischemia or
infarction as the root cause in geriatric patients who sustain trauma. Signs of heart failure
include pulmonary edema with hypoxia, and management includes diuretics and
vasodilators in patients without hypotension.
Postoperative gastrointestinal complications1
Common postoperative gastrointestinal complications include gastrointestinal bleeds,
postoperative ileus, and Clostridium difficile colitis.
Gastrointestinal prophylaxis to minimize the risk of stress ulcers or bleeds typically is limited
to high-risk patients, such as intensive care unit patients.
The presence of a gastrointestinal bleed in elderly patients requires urgent workup because
mortality rates range from 10% to 25%.
Evaluation and management include upper or lower gastrointestinal endoscopy, and
patients should be aggressively resuscitated.
Patients should be evaluated for postoperative ileus via a kidney, ureter, and bladder study.
Medical or surgical evaluation is warranted to evaluate for any mechanical causes of bowel
obstruction that require surgical management.
C difficile colitis occurs if perioperative antibiotic agents alter the normal gut flora and replace
it with C difficile, resulting in a pseudomembranous colitis.
Empiric therapy with oral metronidazole (not severe) or intravenous vancomycin (severe)
should be initiated pending final culture results of the stool.
Criteria for surgical consultation for possible colectomy include a white blood cell count
higher than 20,000 cells/μL and/or a plasma lactate level between 2.2 and 4.0 mmol/L.

Delirium is an substantial postoperative complication of hip fractures and secondary
surgery. The incidence is as high as 30% to 50%. Multiple risk factors play a role in the
development of delirium, including pain, anesthetic agents, infection, and disorientation
from being in an unfamiliar environment. An interdisciplinary approach is key in
preventing and managing delirium. Low-dose narcotics are better in elderly patients.
Peripheral nerve blocks, such as fascia iliaca blocks, may be considered in addition to
other multimodal approaches, such as acetaminophen or NSAIDs.39
Frequent reorientation is important. Keeping windows open during the day and
continually orienting patients help to reduce delirium. If a patient has a hearing aid, he
or she should wear it with all appropriate adaptive/assistive equipment. Having family
present also may be particularly helpful.

In patients with a hip fracture, preoperative optimization to minimize the risk factors for
